title: LATERAL joins
summary: A LATERAL subquery or function in FROM can read columns of the items before it, so it runs per row and may return any number of rows and columns: top-N per group, expanding arrays and series, and naming intermediate expressions.

examples.title: The latest two runs per test case with LEFT JOIN LATERAL

annotations.note: This index matches the subquery's WHERE and ORDER BY. On a large table, each per-test lookup can then read just the newest two index entries and stop, however many runs the test has.

For each test case t, the subquery runs with t.id bound and returns up to two rows of two columns. A scalar subquery in the SELECT list could return one value at most, and a plain join can't apply a LIMIT per group.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true: the correlation lives inside the subquery, so ON has nothing left to test, and true keeps Export CSV with NULLs. CROSS JOIN LATERAL would drop it.
Without LATERAL, each FROM item is evaluated on its own and can't refer to its neighbours, so t.id is an invalid reference (SQLSTATE 42P01).

examples.title: Expanding each row: unnest WITH ORDINALITY and generate_series

annotations.note: unnest is a set-returning function. In FROM, functions may always use columns of earlier items, so LATERAL is optional for them; it is written here for clarity. WITH ORDINALITY (PG 9.4) adds a bigint position starting at 1, so the array's order survives as data.
An empty array produces no rows, so REQ-3 vanished above. LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps it with a NULL tag.
Each sprint expands into one row per day, computed from its own starts and ends. generate_series has no date variant, so the dates are promoted to a timestamp type and d::date converts back.

examples.title: LATERAL as a let binding for computed values

annotations.note: A subquery without FROM computes one row from r's columns. m.ms is now a name that SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY can all use, instead of the same expression written three times.
extract(epoch FROM interval) gives seconds; times 1000 and the cast give whole milliseconds.
ORDER BY may use an output column name (over_budget_ms) because it is evaluated after the SELECT list. WHERE is evaluated before it.
Hence the error: the alias ms doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs (SQLSTATE 42703). Repeating the expression, a subquery or CTE, or the LATERAL above are the ways around it.

use_cases: Top-N per group: latest runs per test case, last three orders per customer
Expanding arrays, jsonb arrays (jsonb_array_elements) and generated series per row
Calling a set-returning function with arguments taken from each row
Naming an intermediate computation once and using it in WHERE and ORDER BY
strengths: Returns several columns and several rows per outer row, which a scalar subquery can't
Top-N per group with ORDER BY ... LIMIT inside can read a few index entries per group, where a window function ranks every row first
Combines with LEFT JOIN ... ON true to keep outer rows that produce nothing
weaknesses: It is a per-row loop: with many outer rows and no supporting index, the subquery runs that many times
CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops outer rows whose subquery or function returns nothing
When nothing depends on the current row, a plain join or a window function says the same thing more simply

pitfalls.title: Correlating in ON instead of inside the subquery
pitfalls.detail: With the condition in ON, the subquery's ORDER BY ... LIMIT 2 picks the newest two runs of the whole table, and ON then keeps only the ones belonging to t. Most test cases get nothing. Put the correlation inside and write ON true.
pitfalls.bad: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM test_runs ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 2) r ON r.test_case_id = t.id
pitfalls.good: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 2) r ON true

pitfalls.title: LIMIT without ORDER BY
pitfalls.detail: Inside the subquery, LIMIT 2 without ORDER BY returns two arbitrary rows. 'Latest' needs an ORDER BY, ideally backed by an index.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL where rows may produce nothing
pitfalls.detail: Empty arrays, test cases without runs and NULL arguments make the outer row disappear. Use LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true when every outer row must stay.

quiz.q: Why `ON true` in `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id ...) last ON true`?
options: The correlation is inside the subquery, and true keeps outer rows without matches
It turns the join into a cross join
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN needs an ON clause; the matching already happened inside, so ON true just preserves outer rows that got no inner rows.

quiz.q: A requirement has tags '{}'. What does `CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(r.tags)` produce for it?
quiz.why: unnest of an empty array returns no rows, and a cross join with nothing is nothing. LEFT JOIN ... ON true would keep it.

quiz.q: Do you need the LATERAL keyword for `FROM requirements r, unnest(r.tags)`?
options: No, function calls in FROM may reference earlier items anyway
quiz.why: For functions the keyword is optional; for subqueries it is required.

quiz.q: Why does `SELECT x * 2 AS y FROM t WHERE y > 10` fail?
options: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list defines y
quiz.why: Output aliases exist only after SELECT is computed; ORDER BY can use them, WHERE can't.

body:
## Concept

A subquery in FROM is normally evaluated independently: it can't see the other items in
the FROM list. Marked `LATERAL`, it may reference columns of the items to its left, so
it is evaluated once for each of their rows, and whatever it returns, zero rows or many,
each with several columns, is joined to that row. Function calls in FROM behave this way
without the keyword.

Three patterns cover most uses: top-N per group (`ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` inside), expanding
a row into several (`unnest`, `generate_series`, `jsonb_array_elements`), and naming a
computed value so later clauses can use it.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- JS/TS: `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` is `flatMap`:
  `cases.flatMap(t => runs.filter(r => r.caseId === t.id).sort(byNewest).slice(0, 2))`.
  `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is the same `flatMap` that emits one padded row when the
  inner list is empty.
- Go: it is the nested loop with a query per row, except it runs as one statement in one
  round trip instead of N+1 queries.
- Python: a nested comprehension where the inner iterable depends on the outer variable:
  `[(t, r) for t in cases for r in latest_runs(t, 2)]`.

## Design notes

Reach for LATERAL when the right-hand side depends on the current row and must return
more than one value. For a single value per row, a scalar subquery reads more simply.
For ranking or running totals over the whole set, window functions (a later module) are
the tool; LATERAL wins for top-N when an index lets each group stop after N rows.

Keep the correlation inside the subquery and the ON clause `true`. A condition moved
into ON is applied after the subquery's LIMIT, which silently changes the answer.

files.examples/01_top_n.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.joins.lateral): a subquery that runs per row and may return many rows.
CREATE TABLE test_cases (id int PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id           int PRIMARY KEY,
  test_case_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES test_cases,
  finished_at  timestamp NOT NULL,
  passed       boolean NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ON test_runs (test_case_id, finished_at DESC);
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES (10, 'Login'), (11, 'Password reset'), (12, 'Export CSV');
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 10, '2026-11-10 09:00', true),
  (2, 10, '2026-11-11 09:00', false),
  (3, 10, '2026-11-12 09:00', true),
  (4, 11, '2026-11-12 10:00', true);

-- The last two runs per test case. The subquery reads t.id: that is LATERAL.
-- LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps test cases that have no runs at all.
SELECT t.title, last.finished_at, last.passed
FROM test_cases t
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT r.finished_at, r.passed
  FROM test_runs r
  WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id
  ORDER BY r.finished_at DESC
  LIMIT 2
) AS last ON true
ORDER BY t.id, last.finished_at DESC;

-- Without the keyword, a FROM subquery cannot see its neighbours.
SELECT t.title, last.finished_at
FROM test_cases t
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT r.finished_at FROM test_runs r
  WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id
  ORDER BY r.finished_at DESC LIMIT 2
) AS last ON true;
files.examples/02_expand_rows.sql:
CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id   int  PRIMARY KEY,
  code text NOT NULL,
  tags text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES
  (1, 'REQ-1', '{security,login}'),
  (2, 'REQ-2', '{export}'),
  (3, 'REQ-3', '{}');

-- A function in FROM is implicitly LATERAL: it takes r.tags as its input and
-- returns one row per element. REQ-3 has no elements, so it drops out.
SELECT r.code, tag.name, tag.pos
FROM requirements r
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(r.tags) WITH ORDINALITY AS tag(name, pos)
ORDER BY r.code, tag.pos;

-- LEFT JOIN ... ON true keeps it, with NULLs.
SELECT r.code, tag.name
FROM requirements r
LEFT JOIN LATERAL unnest(r.tags) AS tag(name) ON true
ORDER BY r.code, tag.name;

-- One row per day of each sprint, generated from that row's own columns.
CREATE TABLE sprints (name text PRIMARY KEY, starts date NOT NULL, ends date NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO sprints VALUES ('S1', '2026-11-02', '2026-11-04'), ('S2', '2026-11-05', '2026-11-06');

SELECT s.name, d::date AS day
FROM sprints s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(s.starts, s.ends, interval '1 day') AS d
ORDER BY d;
files.examples/03_let_binding.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int PRIMARY KEY,
  started_at  timestamp NOT NULL,
  finished_at timestamp NOT NULL,
  budget_ms   int NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, '2026-11-13 09:00:00', '2026-11-13 09:00:01.5', 2000),
  (2, '2026-11-13 09:05:00', '2026-11-13 09:05:04',   3000),
  (3, '2026-11-13 09:10:00', '2026-11-13 09:10:09',   3000);

-- Name an expression once, then use it in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.
SELECT r.id, m.ms, m.ms - r.budget_ms AS over_budget_ms
FROM test_runs r
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT (extract(epoch FROM r.finished_at - r.started_at) * 1000)::int AS ms
) AS m
WHERE m.ms > r.budget_ms
ORDER BY over_budget_ms DESC;

-- A SELECT-list alias can't do that: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT.
SELECT id, (extract(epoch FROM finished_at - started_at) * 1000)::int AS ms
FROM test_runs
WHERE ms > budget_ms;
